stories.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces bipartisan congressional scrutiny over reported China spy link
stories.summary: Lawmakers want to question Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following reports about his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces bipartisan congressional scrutiny over reported China spy link
sources.text: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Some are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about the matter. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers." Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday requesting that he sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang . The reports refer to Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions. Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, The New York Times first reported on Friday. When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times. Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported . Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks. Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X . Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang. Neither Nvidia nor the Commerce Department immediately responded to CNBC's request for comment.

stories.summary: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
sources.text: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion. Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg. In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds. The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago. OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point. The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future. sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as s ources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today. The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others. It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization. Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion. Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double. The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox. OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well. The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing. In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending. Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving. sources.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
sources.text: Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips. Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips. China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times . The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang , was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

sources.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo
sources.text: A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports. The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo . The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo — supposedly based on U.S. intelligence — also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed. An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers. A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm. sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Como usar o mapa do Gemini para encontrar novos lugares?
sources.text: Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 07/11/2026 às 14:00 O Google lançou uma nova ferramenta chamada “Mapa” para o aplicativo Gemini em celulares. Com ela, você pode escolher uma região no mapa e pedir à inteligência artificial informações, recomendações e sugestões relacionadas ao local selecionado. A ferramenta é útil para quem quer encontrar restaurantes, pontos turísticos, lojas ou outros lugares de interesse sem precisar informar apenas o nome de uma cidade ou bairro. Ao abrir o recurso, o Gemini mostra um mapa da região atual do celular com uma área circular destacada . Você pode arrastar o mapa, aproximar ou afastar a visualização para posicionar a área sobre o local que deseja pesquisar. Também dá para procurar outro endereço ou região pelo ícone de lupa no canto superior direito. Depois de encontrar o local desejado, toque em “Explorar esta área”. O Gemini adiciona automaticamente a etiqueta “Área do Mapa” à caixa de texto, indicando que a região selecionada fará parte do contexto da conversa. A partir daí, é só fazer a pergunta ou enviar uma instrução, como pedir restaurantes próximos, pontos turísticos ou lugares interessantes para visitar. O recurso “Mapa” já está disponível nos aplicativos Gemini para Android e iOS , mas ainda não chegou à versão web. A ferramenta aparece no menu aberto pelo botão “+”, ao lado de opções Fotos, Câmera, Avatar, Arquivos, Drive e Notebooks. Caso você não queira adicionar uma região à conversa, basta tocar no botão “X” para fechar o mapa. Confira o passo a passo para começar a usar o mapa no Gemini: Deslize o carrossel de opções até encontrar “Mapa”; Permita que o Gemini acesse sua localização; Arraste o mapa e ajuste o zoom até encontrar a região desejada; Faça perguntas sobre o local ou peça sugestões de lugares para o Gemini. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ 16 comandos para usar o Gemini no Google Maps ”.

sources.title: Cómo usar Gemini para encontrar, analizar y comparar productos antes de comprarlos
sources.text: Aplicaciones como ChatGPT, Claude o Gemini se han convertido en imprescindibles para millones de personas que buscan responder sus preguntas , obtener una explicación sobre algo que no entienden o, simplemente, obtener mejores resultados al buscar por internet . Y si hablamos de búsquedas online, muchas de ellas tienen que ver con comprar un producto o contratar un servicio . De ahí que existan tantos comparadores de viajes, telefonía, compañías eléctricas, electrónica o videojuegos. Es más. Comprar con Gemini o ChatGPT cada vez está más cerca de convertirse en una experiencia todo en uno. Este año hemos visto cómo Google ha ido incorporando elementos relacionados con las compras en sus productos y servicios . Como el carrito universal , que todavía no está presente en todos los países o las constantes mejoras del modo IA de Google y de Gemini enfocadas, precisamente a comprar por internet directamente desde su asistente de inteligencia artificial. Además, ya hemos visto con anterioridad que combinando Gemini y la cámara de tu móvil puedes organizar mejor tus compras . En este artículo vamos a ver de qué manera es posible comprar con Gemini . O, mejor dicho, qué cosas puedes pedirle a la IA de Google para ayudarte durante todo el proceso previo a la compra en sí. Por ejemplo, comparar precios, modelos del mismo producto, encontrar aquello que necesitas, inspirarte si no sabes qué regalar… En definitiva, Gemini puede ser un buen aliado y un asistente de compras si sabes cómo usarlo en tu favor. Comprar con Gemini puede resultar muy cómodo si sabes explicarle bien lo que necesitas . Primero, ¿sabes ya qué vas a comprar? Entonces, pídele que busque la tienda más barata. Si no estás seguro, pregúntale qué producto es mejor entre dos o tres que tengas en mente. Y si no tienes idea de lo que necesitas exactamente, expon tus necesidades y Gemini te dará las soluciones más aproximadas. Aquí van varios ejemplos de prompts sobre compras para empezar: En resumen, al buscar algo en Gemini, deberías tener en cuenta : Gemini nos da una plantilla para hacer una búsqueda de este tipo: “Quiero comprar [producto] para [uso concreto]. Presupuesto: [cantidad]. Debe cumplir: [requisitos imprescindibles]. Prefiero evitar: [restricciones]. Busca opciones disponibles en España, compáralas en una tabla con precio, especificaciones, ventajas, inconvenientes, garantía y reseñas. Después, dame X finalistas, señala riesgos y dime qué comprobaría yo mismo antes de pagar.” Hay muchos parámetros que te hacen decidirte por un producto. Según lo que sea, tal vez te interese lo económico . En otros casos, buscarás que dure mucho y se rompa poco . Otros productos te interesarán más por si tiene piezas de sustitución o recargables baratos . Y, muchas veces, tal vez quieras conocer qué te conviene más si hay que elegir entre que sea bueno, bonito o barato. Así que procura decírselo cuando busques qué comprar con Gemini. Por ejemplo, si vas a comprar algo tan genérico como un teléfono móvil y no tienes un candidato concreto, puedes preguntarle a Gemini que te muestra las mejores opciones según diferentes parámetros : los de mejor calidad, los más económicos, los que mejor combinen calidad-precio… Así, la IA te los mostrará en grupos comparando todas las opciones y te será más fácil decidirte por uno u otro. Las tablas son un elemento visual muy práctico cuando no te decides por un modelo concreto de ese producto que quieres comprar. Si tienes cuatro o cinco opciones a elegir, una tabla te resolverá las dudas. Así que díselo a Gemini, indicando que incluya parámetros como precio final, características más destacadas, dimensiones, peso, garantía… Según qué estés buscando comprar, puedes pedir mil y una cosas que te decantarán por una u otra opción. Materiales de fabricación, opinión de los usuarios y de los expertos, si cumple con los estándares o normativas… No des por sentado que Gemini te va a proporcionar toda la información que necesitas. Especifícalo tú mismo para que la tabla resultante sea lo más completa posible. Cuanto más caro es lo que quieres comprar, más tiempo le dedicarás a la búsqueda . Con Gemini ocurre igual. Si se trata de comprar con Gemini algo que te supondrá un desembolso considerable de dinero, te conviene utilizar la función Deep Research . En castellano, investigación profunda. Le llevará más tiempo a la IA darte una respuesta. Pero esa respuesta será un informe más preciso sobre lo que estás buscando. Y merece la pena. Además, en el modo Deep Research de Gemini puedes incluir tus propias fuentes . Por ejemplo, buscando tus propias fuentes en Google o subiendo archivos de manuales, prospectos, catálogos o folletos de productos. Así te asegurarás de que la IA busque donde tú quieres y te dé la información acorde a fuentes que tú consideres fiables o de confianza. Dedícale tiempo a esto antes de lanzar tu pregunta a Gemini y obtendrás mejores respuestas . Otra manera de ayudarte a decidirte entre dos o tres productos similares consiste en ver qué dicen los demás. Aunque las reseñas y opiniones tienen sus más y sus menos, y a veces hay que cogerlas con pinzas, pueden servir de ayuda. Así que pídele a Gemini que te diga qué opiniones merecen en internet determinado producto y si hay quejas o polémicas . Esto sirve tanto para el producto o servicio como para la tienda o proveedor del servicio . Hay tiendas y comercios en los que confiamos a ciegas. Pero es posible que encuentres un nuevo sitio con buenos precios que quieras probar. Si no lo conoces, necesitarás opiniones favorables que te hagan confiar en él. O, al contrario, que te libren de una mala experiencia. Pregunta si la compra es segura , si el envío es correcto, si hay atención al cliente , sede física, si el servicio posterior a la compra es el adecuado… Toda precaución es poca cuando se trata de comprar. Especialmente si el coste del producto es alto. Cuando ya tengas seguro qué producto quieres, ya puedes empezar la segunda fase: comparar prec

stories.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference
stories.summary: Together Compiler uses agents and persistent engines to optimize open models in under 24 hours, delivering up to 3.7x higher throughput as traffic changes.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference
sources.text: AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand. Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation. In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today. As an inference provider, we see a variety of user behaviors based on regional patterns, new model releases, and burstiness. It’s clear that we must adapt to ever-changing user behavior with specialized optimizations for each new deployment. TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine. 1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization ‍ Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes , significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts. 2. TKCC balances the tradeoff between measurement throughput and measurement fidelity ‍ Existing agent optimization systems either iteratively relaunch the inference engine, suffering from low experiment throughput, or optimize standalone kernels in isolation, outside of the inference engine, suffering from poor measurement fidelity. Systems that optimize standalone kernels often evaluate them using random input data. However, with modern architectures using data-dependent primitives like MoE and sparse-k attention, input data distributions have a direct effect on which optimization strategies may win (see figure below). High-fidelity inputs are important for effective optimization. TKCC uses a tier of persistent engines to balance the throughput-fidelity tradeoff: “fast engines” load a few layers and are ideal for rapid iteration and low-variance timings, while “slower engines” load many layers and are ideal for testing whether optimizations hold-up on real data distributions. 3. TKCC utilizes a custom cost model to select parallelism strategies (e.g., TP, EP, DCP, etc.) for agents to achieve the highest performance Existing systems have sophisticated methods for selecting inference configurations under SLA requirements. However, selecting the ideal configuration faces the same throughput-fidelity tradeoff: it is intractable to measure each parallelism configuration, especially because software implementations are immature. A naive approach is to select a parallelism strategy based on raw hardware specs or micro-benchmarks. However, this insufficiently captures data dependent traffic properties like MoE expert imbalance or uneven prompt length distributions. We designed a cost model that uses a tiered measurement strategy involving hardware specs, microbenchmarks, and measured forward passes to construct a high-fidelity representation while rapidly pruning the configuration search space to support continual traffic drift. We evaluate TKCC against three different types of baselines: Hand-tuned megakernels, InferenceX engine configurations, and popular AI codebases from diverse domains like weather modeling, PDE, time series and biology models. We start by evaluating the canonical MegaKernel workload: Llama 1B at batch size 1. This model architecture has been well-optimized by both human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. TKCC generates 1.7x higher TPS and continues to perform as sequence length increases. We evaluate TKCC on the AgentX benchmark from SemiAnalysis. We start from the best-reported open source engine configurations for frontier models across inference engines and hardware platforms. TKCC consistently sets the performance frontier across all settings, outperforming highly-optimized baselines by up to 2.6x higher TPS. 1 We also evaluate specifically on the low-latency use case at batch size 1 and set the state-of-the-art performance with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. For these results, we use our cost model to select the parallelism configuration instead of using the InferenceX configuration. We observe speedups with this approach. We select popular open-source code bases across weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology. We show the geometric mean speedups of TKCC over simply using Claude Code with the /goal command, illustrating that the principles of TKCC generalize across domains. We have been using TKCC as a general purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference. For Together AI, the most exciting systems challenge has been Polymorphic Inference .

stories.title: Polymorphic Inference: self-tuning inference for open models
stories.summary: Models, traffic and chips are constantly changing. Polymorphic Inference adapts to each, and Together Compiler uses AI agents to keep production inference tuned.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: Polymorphic Inference: self-tuning inference for open models
sources.text: At Together AI, we focus on making AI abundantly available to every individual user and organization. Our research team – the researchers behind FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, ThunderAgent, and more – has been a key driver behind our inference excellence. As the inference market grows exponentially, we’ve been focusing on how to scale our research capacity to enable abundant intelligence for all. This has required a shift in our thinking from Static Inference to Polymorphic Inference – which is our response to the velocity of new model releases, diversity of model architectures, fast-changing workloads, and fast-changing hardware platforms. In this blog, we’ll highlight our research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era – and how we are continuously using AI agents to optimize their own inference with Continuous Compilation . Over the past year, there has been a marked step change in the diversity of open-source models and the ways that these models are deployed in production environments. We see this step change as requiring a new approach that we call Polymorphic Inference . Polymorphic Inference (inference in “many shapes” from Greek) is a response to a number of changes we are seeing across the industry, for us primarily defined by the convergence of a few trends: Polymorphic Inference is our response to these changes – inference that changes and adapts to these rapidly-changing environments. We contrast this against the state of the world before the explosion of OSS inference – which we retroactively call the era of “Static Inference.” Whereas modern Polymorphic Inference takes on infinite different shapes, Static Inference is defined by closed models, traditional Transformer architectures, single-user, and single-hardware-platform inference. One of our motivations behind writing this blog post is that a lot of the discourse around inference systems remains quite focused on the legacy Static Inference paradigm. We take some of the blame here! For a long time, it has been possible to write kernels that are optimal for a variety of settings. FlashAttention, near and dear to our hearts, is still one of the best ways to run training workloads and many prefill workloads. And nearly two years ago we wrote about megakernels for AI inference, a single kernel painstakingly designed around a single static shape (e.g., batch size one Llama 1B). But through the experience of putting some of the first megakernels into production for our customers last year, we learned an interesting lesson: megakernel fusion is actually not the right design goal for modern Polymorphic Inference! In the era of Polymorphic Inference, every variation – from model architecture (e.g. MoE), to workload (dynamic workloads larger than batch size 1) – requires different technical approaches. At Together, we are systems and AI researchers at heart – so we view this as an incredibly exciting time to be rethinking our research agenda for this bright new future. ‍ So, what’s the solution when your production traffic becomes ever more diverse? Get the AI agents to optimize themselves. This is the RSI moment for OSS models! Achieving Polymorphic Inference requires solving a number of technical challenges in how we serve models. An ideal Polymorphic Inference experience is one that responds to the rapidly changing landscape of model architectures and workloads. These are lofty goals, but we believe that they are worth striving for. For us, one of the keys to achieving these goals is getting AI agents to help optimize themselves . The RSI loop is here for OSS models! One of the projects that we’re announcing today as a first step towards achieving our goals for Polymorphic Inference is Together Compiler , a rapid AI-powered performance optimization RSI loop. Today, Together Compiler powers Continuous Compilation optimization loops across many of our top production inference workloads. Together Compiler takes the classic challenge of optimizing inference workloads and recasts it from a traditional compiler translation problem to an agentic search problem. Together Compiler identifies a core set of key optimization patterns and pairs a swarm of agents with a high-fidelity persistent engine for fast iterations. This work was the result of many months of work by Together’s Frontier Performance team, notably from Reyna Abhyankar and Dylan Lim! Together Compiler is running in production today on some of our most popular serverless endpoints, where it has found further gains on top of already highly optimized code. Excitingly, Together Compiler gives us the ability to quickly adapt to rapidly changing model architectures and traffic workloads. We call this capability Continuous Compilation . Whereas previously new workloads would require new sets of hand-written kernels and optimizations, Continuous Compilation driven by Together Compiler means that we can automatically adapt to new traffic shapes and workloads. We’ve learned a ton scaling Together AI to serve trillions of tokens per day (and for the first time even serving more tokens than closed-source model labs on OpenRouter earlier in October!). This has informed our vision and research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era. Here’s a little preview of some of the things coming up on our research agenda: Self-serve Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler ‍ Performance optimization needs to be a function of the workload deployment: the model, engine, traffic shape, and customer use case. Soon, our customers will be able to use Together Compiler to optimize their dedicated endpoints for their unique workloads at the click of a button. Together Compiler is available to end customers in limited beta today – reach out if you want early access!
